newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian UCB bids to make euro bank notes.
newsitem.headline: Belgian UCB bids to make euro bank notes.

text.p: Belgian chemicals and drugs group UCB said on Wednesday it was talking to the European Monetary Institute (EMI) about producing a polymer film-based euro bank note.
"I can confirm we are talking to the EMI and other central banks about polymer bank notes," UCB spokesman Alain Douxchamps said. He declined to give details.

Douxchamps was commenting on an article in Wednesday's Financial Times that said UCB's British films division based in Wigton, Cumbria, had formed a joint venture with Australia's central bank to supply the plastic notes to other central banks.

UCB and The Reserve Bank of Australia set up a joint venture in January to commercialise the polymer film bank note technology, which is already used in notes in Australia, Singapore, Western Samoa, Brunei, New Guinea and Kuwait.
"We think the polymer bank note has a lot to offer. It lasts four times longer than paper. It is also much more difficult to counterfeit," Douxchamps said.
Polymer film-based bank notes in use in Australia leave a small window of film exposed which appears black in photocopies.
UCB estimates the market for polymer-based banknotes could be worth 500 million Belgian francs by the year 2000.

That forecast was based on UCB being able to sell the technology to a number of central banks, not necessarily including the future European Central Bank, of which the EMI is the precursor, Douxchamps said.
UCB's bank note polymer films presently account for around 100 million francs of annual sales. The films division as a whole was expected to have sales in 1996 of 10 billion francs.
"It's a small part of our total turnover of the film division, but it's a speciality product with a high added value," Douxchamps said.
